records.title: Theseus and the Minotaur of the Cretan Labyrinth
records.summary: To end the tribute of seven youths and seven maidens sent every nine years from Athens to be devoured by the Minotaur—a monstrous beast with the head of a bull and the body of a man—young prince Theseus volunteers as a tribute to Crete. At the palace of Knossos, King Minos's daughter, Ariadne, falls in love with him and provides a sword and a ball of golden thread (clue) to navigate Daedalus's winding subterranean maze. After slaying the beast in the darkest recesses of the labyrinth, Theseus follows the thread back to safety and escapes with the Athenian hostages, sailing home toward the Aegean.
alternate_names: Theseus and the Bull of Minos
records.historical_period: Classical Greek Era (recorded in Apollodorus's Bibliotheca c. 2nd Century BCE)

records.title: Daedalus and the Tragic Flight of Icarus
records.summary: Imprisoned within a high seaside tower on Crete by King Minos so that the secrets of the Labyrinth would never be revealed, the master inventor Daedalus fashions two pairs of magnificent wings from bird feathers bound together with beeswax and thread for himself and his youthful son Icarus. Before launching from the cliffs over the Aegean, Daedalus sternly cautions Icarus to maintain a middle course: flying too low will dampen the feathers with sea spray, while flying too high will melt the wax under the blazing sun. Intoxicated by the freedom of flight, Icarus soars toward Apollo's chariot; the wax dissolves, and he plunges to his death into the sea, ever after called the Icarian Sea.
records.historical_period: Classical Antiquity (preserved in Ovid's Metamorphoses Book VIII c. 8 CE)
records.region_or_community: Crete and the Icarian Sea, Aegean Islands

records.title: Perseus and the Severed Head of Medusa
records.summary: Commanded by the tyrannical king Polydectes to bring back the head of the Gorgon Medusa, whose terrifying gaze turns any living creature instantly to stone, the young hero Perseus is aided by the Olympian gods. Hermes equips him with a curved adamantine sickle, while Athena provides a polished bronze shield to view the monster's reflection safely without looking into her eyes. Receiving winged sandals and the helm of invisibility from the Stygian nymphs, Perseus flies across the ocean to the Gorgons' lair. Decapitating Medusa while she sleeps, the winged horse Pegasus springs from her severed neck, and Perseus preserves the head to rescue Andromeda from a sea monster.

records.title: Orpheus and Eurydice: The Backward Glance into Hades
records.summary: When his beloved bride Eurydice dies of a viper bite on their wedding day, the peerless Thracian musician Orpheus descends into the gloomy underworld of Hades to plead for her soul. Playing his lyre, his divine melodies move the three-headed hound Cerberus to sleep, halt the tortures of Tantalus, and cause King Hades and Queen Persephone to weep iron tears. Hades grants permission for Eurydice to follow Orpheus back into the sunlight on one inviolable condition: he must walk ahead and never look back at her until both have reached the upper world. Just as he steps into the daylight, overcome by love and doubt, Orpheus turns to gaze at her; Eurydice is dragged back into the shadows forever.
records.historical_period: Classical Antiquity (Virgil's Georgics IV and Ovid's Metamorphoses X)
records.region_or_community: Thrace and the Underworld portals of Cape Matapan

records.title: Prometheus and the Sacred Gift of Fire
records.summary: Taking pity on fragile, shivering mortals who dwelt like ants in dark caves without craft or knowledge, the wise Titan Prometheus defied the supreme Olympian decree of Zeus. Ascending Mount Olympus, Prometheus concealed a glowing spark of divine celestial fire inside the hollow stem of a giant fennel stalk (narthex) and brought the flame down to humanity. With fire, mankind forged metal tools, built civilization, and mastered the arts. In wrath, Zeus had Prometheus chained to a jagged precipice in the Caucasus Mountains, where a giant eagle tore at his liver each day, which regenerated each night, until Heracles broke the chains.
records.historical_period: Archaic Greece (c. 5th Century BCE Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound)

records.title: Jason and the Golden Fleece of Colchis
records.summary: To reclaim his rightful throne of Iolcos from his treacherous uncle Pelias, young prince Jason commands the Argo, a magical fifty-oared vessel constructed by Argus with a speaking oak timber from Dodona, crewed by the greatest heroes of Greece (the Argonauts). Journeying through the crashing rocks of the Symplegades into the Black Sea, Jason arrives in the distant kingdom of Colchis to demand the Golden Fleece of the winged ram Chrysomallos. Aided by the sorceress princess Medea, who provides magical protective salves, Jason yokes fire-breathing bronze-hoofed bulls, sows dragon's teeth that sprout armed warriors, and lulls the sleepless dragon guardian to sleep.
records.historical_period: Hellenistic Era (c. 3rd Century BCE Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica)

records.title: The Labours of Heracles: The Nemean Lion and the Lernean Hydra
records.summary: To atone for a fit of madness cast upon him by the goddess Hera, the supreme hero Heracles (Hercules) is bound to serve King Eurystheus of Tiryns, who assigns him twelve impossible labors. In his first labor in Nemea, Heracles confronts a monstrous lion whose golden pelt is impervious to bronze, stone, and iron; wrestling the beast bare-handed, he strangles it to death and fashions its impenetrable skin into his iconic cloak. In his second labor in the swamps of Lerna, he battles the venomous nine-headed Hydra; with the assistance of his nephew Iolaus, who cauterizes the severed necks with burning brands to prevent double heads from sprouting, Heracles slays the monster and dips his arrows in its lethal venom.
records.historical_period: Archaic to Classical Greece (Hesiod and Apollodorus)

records.title: The Gorgon Sister of Alexander the Great
records.summary: In widespread modern Greek maritime folklore, Alexander the Great sought the Water of Immortality (Athanato Nero) to achieve eternal life, carrying the water in a flask. While he was away, his sister Thessalonike inadvertently spilled the flask, or used it to wash wild onions. In desperation, she drank the remaining drops and was transformed into a mermaid (Gorgona) with the torso of a woman and the scaly tail of a great fish, condemned to swim the Aegean Sea. When storm squalls rock a ship, she rears from the foam, grasps the prow, and asks the captain: 'Is King Alexander alive?' The only answer to calm the tempest is: 'He lives and reigns, and conquers the world!' Any other answer causes her to capsize the vessel.
alternate_names: The Legend of the Aegean Gorgona
records.historical_period: Byzantine to Modern Greek Maritime Tradition
records.region_or_community: Aegean Sea, Cyclades, and Dodecanese Islands

records.title: The Nereids of the Mountain Springs (Neraides)
records.summary: Surviving directly from ancient nymphs into modern Greek rural folklore, Neraides (Nereids) are beautiful, ethereal maiden spirits who dwell in secluded mountain springs, grottoes, ravines, and beneath wild plane trees. Clad in diaphanous white silk robes, they dance in circular rings at high noon and midnight to the piping of supernatural panpipes. Village folklore cautions shepherds never to disturb their dance or drink from their springs without making an offering of bread or sugar. Anyone who enters their circle is struck dumb (vovos), loses their shadow, or is lured into madness by their enchanting songs.
records.historical_period: Classical Antiquity through Living Modern Greek Rural Folklore
records.region_or_community: Arcadia, Mount Parnassus, and the Peloponnese highlands

records.title: The Vrykolakas of Santorini: The Undead of the Cyclades
records.summary: A prominent figure of Greek island folklore, the Vrykolakas is an animated corpse that refuses to decompose in its volcanic grave, swollen like an inflated drum and knocking on village doors at midnight. Calling out the name of householders once, anyone who answers the knock falls ill and dies within days. Historically, the volcanic island of Santorini (Thira) was regarded as the capital of the Vrykolakas, where neighboring Aegean islands sent stubborn cadavers for burial because the sulfurous volcanic ash was believed to bind restless spirits. In 1700, French botanist Joseph Pitton de Tournefort famously documented the formal exhumation and ritual cremation of an alleged Vrykolakas on Mykonos.
records.historical_period: Ottoman Greece Era (documented 1700 by Tournefort, active 18th–19th Century)
